issues.legal_issue: A statutory revisional court may not rehear a case or replace concurrent factual findings merely because it would assess the evidence differently, absent a defect amounting to a miscarriage of justice or a decision not according to law.
material_facts: A landlord brought an eviction suit alleging that the tenant had sublet part of the premises without the required written consent.
The trial court found that the sub-tenancy began after the relevant rent-control law came into force and that the landlord had not consented; the appellate court affirmed those factual findings.

In revision, the High Court concluded that the sub-tenancy had begun earlier after reassessing the evidence, including on the mistaken belief that the appellate court had not considered a relevant petition.

The appellate court had considered that petition and relied on the tenant’s admission in another proceeding; the High Court identified no defect in the trial or other miscarriage of justice warranting revision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in substituting its assessment of the evidence for the concurrent factual findings. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s revisional order was set aside, and the appellate court’s order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The majority held that sections 34 and 35(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 distinguish an appeal, which ordinarily permits rehearing on law and fact, from revision, which does not create a right to rehearing. The words “according to law” in section 35(1) concern the decision as a whole and permit intervention to prevent a miscarriage of justice, but do not permit interference merely because the revisional court might have reached a different factual conclusion. The majority approved the formulation in Bell & Co. Ltd. v. Waman Hemraj, (1938) 40 Bom. L.R. 125. Section 13(1)(b)(i) was relevant to the underlying allegation of subletting without written consent. Kapur J. agreed with the result but considered the revisional power wider: in his view it could reach, among other things, a merits-affecting legal error, manifest injustice, ignored material evidence, or a finding unsupported by any legitimate inference, while still not turning revision into an appeal on facts.

rule.if: statutory_revision_without_further_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and (revision_reweighs_evidence or revision_relies_on_mistaken_record_assumption) and no_miscarriage_or_legality_defect

predicates.statutory_revision_without_further_appea: A party challenged a lower court decision through statutory revision where the governing scheme provided no further appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual finding.
predicates.revision_reweighs_evidence: The revisional court reassessed the evidence to reach a different factual conclusion.
predicates.revision_relies_on_mistaken_record_assum: The revisional court acted on an assumption about the record that was incorrect.
predicates.no_miscarriage_or_legality_defect: The record disclosed no defect in the proceedings or decision amounting to a miscarriage of justice or otherwise requiring intervention.

issues.definition: When a statutory revision with no further appeal follows concurrent factual findings, and the revisional court reweighs evidence or relies on a mistaken assumption about the record without a miscarriage of justice or legality defect, its interference is unjustified.
